issues.legal_issue: A residence previously shared by spouses is not a shared household against an in-law merely because the spouses lived there, where the husband has no ownership or tenancy interest and the home is not joint-family property of which he is a member.
material_facts: The wife lived with her husband in a house owned exclusively by her mother-in-law.
The husband neither owned nor rented the house, and the house was not joint-family property of which he was a member.
The wife had lived in the house during the marriage but later left it and sought a right to reside there.
issues.conclusion: The house was not a shared household within the meaning of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, and the wife could not claim a right to reside there under that Act.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(s) and 17(1) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, read sensibly, do not make every place where spouses once lived a shared household. A shared household for this purpose is a house belonging to or rented by the husband, or a house belonging to a joint family of which the husband is a member. An interpretation that would make all relatives’ homes where spouses had previously stayed shared households would produce an absurd result.

rule.if: domestic_violence_residence_claim and past_spousal_co_residence and home_exclusively_owned_by_inlaw and husband_has_no_ownership_or_tenancy and home_not_joint_family_property

predicates.domestic_violence_residence_claim: The claimant sought a residence right in a proceeding concerning domestic violence.
predicates.past_spousal_co_residence: The claimant and the claimant’s spouse had lived together in the home at some time.
predicates.home_exclusively_owned_by_inlaw: The home was owned exclusively by the spouse’s relative rather than by the spouse.
predicates.husband_has_no_ownership_or_tenancy: The husband had neither an ownership interest nor a tenancy in the home.
predicates.home_not_joint_family_property: The home was not joint-family property of a family of which the husband was a member.

issues.definition: When a residence claim under domestic-violence law concerns a home once shared by spouses but exclusively owned by an in-law, not owned or rented by the husband, and not joint-family property of which he is a member, the home is not a shared household for the claimed residence right.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for alternative accommodation under a domestic-violence residence order lies against the husband, not against his in-laws or other relatives.
material_facts: The wife sought alternative accommodation under Section 19(1)(f) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.
The residence claim was directed against her husband’s parents, including the owner of the house in dispute.
issues.conclusion: The wife could claim alternative accommodation only against her husband, not against her in-laws or other relatives.
issues.legal_principle: Section 19(1)(f) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, permits an order for alternative accommodation or rent, but the Court held that such a claim can be made only against the husband, not his in-laws or other relatives.

predicates.alternative_accommodation_claim_in_resid: The claimant sought alternative accommodation or rent as part of a residence-order proceeding.
predicates.claim_directed_against_inlaw: The claimant directed the alternative-accommodation claim against the spouse’s relative rather than the spouse.

issues.definition: If alternative accommodation is sought in a residence-order proceeding against a spouse’s relative, the claim lies only against the spouse.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who is not in possession cannot obtain an injunction against dispossession, and a factual finding of non-possession is not open to interference in constitutional supervisory review.
material_facts: The wife sought an injunction concerning her asserted right to occupy the house.
The Senior Civil Judge found that she was not residing in the house and dismissed her temporary-injunction application.
That finding was challenged in proceedings under Article 227 of the Constitution.
issues.conclusion: Because the wife was not in possession, she could not obtain an injunction restraining the owners from dispossessing her; the finding of non-possession could not be interfered with in the supervisory proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the finding that the claimant was not residing in the premises as a finding of fact that could not be interfered with under Articles 226 or 227 of the Constitution. It further held that a person not in possession cannot claim an injunction restraining dispossession from the property.

rule.if: injunction_claim_depends_on_current_possession and claimant_not_in_possession and non_possession_is_factual_finding and constitutional_supervisory_review

predicates.injunction_claim_depends_on_current_poss: The claimant sought an injunction protecting possession or preventing dispossession from a home.
predicates.claimant_not_in_possession: The claimant was not in possession of the home when the injunction claim was considered.
predicates.non_possession_is_factual_finding: A lower court found as a matter of fact that the claimant was not residing in or possessing the home.
predicates.constitutional_supervisory_review: The challenge to that factual finding was brought in constitutional supervisory proceedings.

issues.definition: When an injunction against dispossession depends on current possession, the claimant is found not to be in possession, and that finding is challenged in constitutional supervisory review, the injunction cannot be granted.

issues.legal_issue: A spouse has no general right to occupy a matrimonial home owned by an in-law merely because the home was the couple’s matrimonial residence.
material_facts: The wife claimed a right to continue living in the house where she had lived with her husband after marriage.
The house belonged to her mother-in-law, not to her husband.
The Court found no applicable Indian law giving the wife a general occupation right in that house against her mother-in-law.
issues.conclusion: The wife had no right to live in the house merely because it had been her matrimonial home.
issues.legal_principle: In B.R. Mehta v. Atma Devi, [1987] 4 SCC 183, this Court observed that a right of occupation in a matrimonial home might be desirable, but the Court held that this observation expressed hope and did not lay down law. Unlike the English Matrimonial Homes Act, 1967, no such general right existed in India; courts cannot create or amend the law, and any rights available under law could be asserted against the husband, not his parents.

rule.if: spousal_matrimonial_home_occupation_claim and home_owned_by_inlaw and claim_is_against_inlaw and no_applicable_law_grants_general_occupation_right

predicates.spousal_matrimonial_home_occupation_clai: A spouse claimed the right to occupy a home because the couple had lived there as their matrimonial residence.
predicates.home_owned_by_inlaw: The home was owned by a relative of the claimant’s spouse.
predicates.claim_is_against_inlaw: The claimant asserted the occupation right against the spouse’s relative rather than against the spouse.
predicates.no_applicable_law_grants_general_occupat: No applicable law granted a general right to occupy the home on the basis of its status as a matrimonial residence.

issues.definition: If a spouse claims occupation of a matrimonial home owned by an in-law against that in-law, and no applicable law grants a general occupation right, matrimonial-home status alone creates no occupation right against the in-law.
